name: common_feature_matching
hypothesis: People abstract the set of features that every example has in common (parity, divisibility, being a square/cube/prime/power, final digit, decade) and say "yes" to a target in proportion to how many of those shared features it also has. This is a feature-matching (common-feature contrast) process with no size principle: a rule-like feature shared by all examples is extended to any number that has it, however far away, and adding examples only matters by removing features that are no longer shared.

name: tempered_size_principle
hypothesis: People infer the hidden concept by Bayesian reasoning over the same mathematical rules and numerical intervals, but they apply the size principle only weakly: each example favours smaller concepts by a fractional power of their size rather than in full proportion. As a result broad rules such as "even" or "ends in 7" keep their strength against narrower rules and tight intervals, so the model disagrees most sharply with the current best model on far-away targets that fit a broad rule (e.g. distant even numbers for an all-even set), which it predicts people will endorse much more often, and on near-but-off-rule targets, which it predicts they will endorse less.

name: common_feature_profile_matching
hypothesis: People judge membership by common-feature matching rather than by probabilistic concept induction: they notice which arithmetic and surface properties (parity, being a multiple, power, square or prime, a final digit, a digit it contains, its decade) every example shares, and say yes in proportion to how much of that shared profile the target also has, with more distinctive (rarer) shared properties counting more. Numerical proximity plays no role, and there is no size-principle tightening with more examples beyond what changes the shared profile.

name: tempered_size_principle_mixture
hypothesis: Refinement of `bigelow_piantadosi_mixture`: people do the same Bayesian concept learning over the same 45 rules and all intervals of 1-100, but they apply the size principle only partially — the evidence from the examples is tempered by a single fitted exponent, so a few examples that happen to sit close together do not overwhelm a broad rule such as "even" or "ends in 2" the way strict strong sampling would. The one change is this evidence-weighting exponent (sharpness of the size principle), which shifts belief toward broad rules when examples share a regularity and lets generalisation tighten less with more examples.

name: memory_limited_example_recall
hypothesis: People do Bayesian concept learning over arithmetic rules and numerical intervals, but they reason from an imperfect memory of the examples: each example is independently retained with some probability, and they generalise from only the examples they hold in mind. Because a judgement is often based on one or two of the examples rather than all of them, a target that shares a property (such as a final digit or a divisor) with just one example is often endorsed, and generalisation tightens less with more examples than an ideal learner who uses every example would predict.

name: example_subset_memory_bayes
hypothesis: People do Bayesian concept learning over the same arithmetic rules and numerical intervals as an ideal learner (strong sampling, size principle), but under a working-memory limit: each example shown enters their inference only with some fitted probability, so they often generalise from just a subset of the examples. Reasoning from one or two remembered examples lets a rule shared by only some examples (e.g. "ends in 3" from 23 in {16, 23}) win, and weakens the size-principle tightening that more examples would normally produce.

name: exemplar_digit_feature_similarity
hypothesis: People judge membership by surface-feature similarity to the individual examples, not by inducing a rule shared by the whole set: they compare the target with each example on a few salient digit and arithmetic features (its last digit, its tens digit, its parity, and its remainder when divided by three), and the more features the target shares with a given example the more similar it feels, with similarity falling off exponentially with the number of mismatching features. The yes probability grows with the target's average similarity to the examples, so a target that shares only its final digit with one example (in a set without a common final digit) still earns credit, and plain numerical distance plays no role beyond sharing a tens digit.

name: exception_tolerant_tempered_mixture
hypothesis: Refinement of `tempered_size_principle_mixture`: people do the same tempered Bayesian concept learning over the same 45 rules and all intervals of 1-100, but they believe the program often slips and produces a number outside its concept, so they tolerate exceptions — the fraction of examples assumed to be off-concept noise is a fitted parameter instead of a fixed 10%. The one change is this fitted exception rate: when most but not all examples share a regularity (e.g. three of four end in 2), the rule that covers the majority survives the exception, so people extend a partly shared last digit or arithmetic property to distant targets, and lean less on tight numerical intervals, than a learner who treats every example as strictly from the concept.

name: tempered_size_principle_digit_unions

The one change is this graded, frequency-weighted profile (its steepness fitted by one exponent), so a target that shares a final digit or another property with only some of the examples still gains support — closing the critique that people endorse partial last-digit matches far more than the incumbent predicts.

So the same examples shown in a different order lead to different generalisations — an example that breaks the others' pattern is discounted less when it comes in the favoured position, and people generalise around it more.

hypothesis: People judge membership by how similar the target looks, as a written numeral, to each example: similarity falls off exponentially with the number of digit edits (substitutions, insertions or deletions of a digit) needed to turn the target's numeral into an example's, and the yes probability grows with the target's average similarity across the examples. This soft-threshold decision rule makes answers more all-or-none than the graded posterior (near-unanimous yes for well-supported targets, near-unanimous no for weakly supported ones), with a fitted criterion setting an overall bias toward yes or no.

name: rule_or_range_union

They expect such an add-on stretch to be a short range of moderate width placed anywhere that covers the off-rule example (not necessarily centred on it, with point-sized and very wide add-ons a priori less likely), so when one example breaks the others' shared pattern people endorse a whole run of numbers around that outlier, of either parity, while still extending the rule to distant numbers and rejecting rule-breaking neighbours of the majority examples.

name: isolation_weighted_exemplar_memory
hypothesis: People do not infer a concept: they store each example as a separate exemplar and say yes in proportion to the target's average similarity to the stored examples, where similarity falls off with distance on a compressed mental number line and with mismatches in final digit and in parity. Exemplars are not stored equally strongly — an example that is isolated, sharing its final digit with none of the other examples (the one odd-one-out in the set), is remembered more vividly (a von Restorff isolation effect), so it carries more weight in the comparison and people generalise to its neighbours more than to equally close neighbours of the conforming examples.

name: parity_markedness_odd_cost
hypothesis: People code parity asymmetrically: "even" (divisible by two) is the default, unmarked concept, while "odd" is represented as its negation ("not divisible by two"), so considering it carries an extra cognitive cost that lowers its prior plausibility; otherwise they infer the program's concept as the best tempered, exception-tolerant Bayesian learner does (salient final-digit rules, moderate-width ranges, rule-plus-neighbourhood exceptions around an off-pattern example emitted through a side channel). Because of this cost, when a set mixes odd and even examples, "even, plus an exception around the odd one" beats "odd, plus an exception around the even one", so people endorse even targets more than odd ones, and they extend all-odd sets to distant odd numbers less readily than all-even sets to distant even numbers.

name: weak_sampling_doubt
hypothesis: People reason like the best Bayesian concept learner (tempered, exception-tolerant inference over salient final-digit and other rules, moderate-width ranges on a compressed number line, and rule-plus-neighbourhood exceptions around an off-pattern example emitted through a side channel), with one distortion: they are not fully convinced the examples were produced by the program itself, and give some fitted weight to the possibility that the numbers were picked arbitrarily and merely confirmed to belong. Under that "picked, not produced" reading, a concept's size carries no evidential cost, so people discount the size principle — most when the examples fit both small and large concepts — and generalise more broadly than an ideal strong-sampling learner, extending to large rules, wide ranges and wide regions around an outlier example.

name: even_leaning_rule_prior
hypothesis: People expect a number-producing program to be "about" even numbers more readily than about odd ones: in their prior over candidate rules, a rule is more plausible the larger the share of its members that are even (so "even", "multiples of 4", "powers of 2", "ends in 6" start ahead of "odd", "ends in 7", "powers of 3" or "primes"), while otherwise doing the same tempered, exception-tolerant Bayesian concept learning as the best model (salient final-digit rules, moderate-width ranges on a compressed number line, and rule-plus-neighbourhood exceptions anchored on an off-pattern example and emitted through a side channel). Because ranges are parity-neutral, this even-leaning rule prior shows up wherever the examples leave both parities open — most clearly in sets mixing odd and even examples, where even-based rule-plus-exception concepts win and people endorse even non-example targets more than odd ones.

name: gamma_shaped_range_width_prior

name: even_salient_pedagogical_teacher
hypothesis: Refinement of `pedagogical_teacher_sampling`: people do the same helpful-teacher concept learning (they expect a teacher to pick unambiguous examples) over the same rules, ranges and example-anchored rule-plus-neighbourhood exceptions, but "even numbers" is a more natural, more readily entertained concept than "odd numbers", so the even rule gets its own fitted prior boost on top of the shared parity/final-digit salience. The one change is this even-over-odd asymmetry in the rule prior: when a set mixes odd and even examples people lean towards "even, with an exception" and endorse even non-example targets more than odd ones (the critique's mixed-parity even-target bias), and they extend all-even sets to distant evens more readily than all-odd sets to distant odds.

name: range_plus_exception_side_channel
hypothesis: Refinement of `anchored_neighbourhood_side_channel`: people do the same tempered, exception-tolerant Bayesian concept learning (salient final-digit rules, moderate-width ranges on a compressed number line, and "rule plus exception" programs whose side channel emits a small fuzzy neighbourhood around an off-pattern example), but the main channel of such a "program plus exception" can also be a range of numbers, not only an arithmetic rule: "numbers from 20 to 35, and now and then something around 87". The one change is this range-plus-exception program, which takes the same share of prior belief, the same neighbourhood radii and the same side-channel rate as the rule version. So when most examples cluster on the number line and one lies far away, people fill in the cluster's stretch and also endorse the outlier's close neighbours, while rejecting the empty gap between them, instead of falling back on one wide range or on a rule.

name: pattern_violation_anchored_exception
hypothesis: People read the examples in the order shown and only treat an example as an exception when it breaks a pattern that earlier examples have already set up: they do the same tempered, exception-tolerant Bayesian concept learning as the best model (salient final-digit rules, moderate-width ranges on a compressed number line, and "rule plus a fuzzy neighbourhood around an off-pattern example" programs emitted through a side channel), but the exception neighbourhood can be centred only on an off-rule example that comes after at least one example the rule covers. So an off-pattern example shown first, before any pattern exists, is never singled out as the program's exception, and people generalise to its close neighbours less than they would if the same outlier came later in the list.

name: nearest_example_radius_concepts
hypothesis: People's magnitude-based guesses about the program are similarity neighbourhoods around the examples, not stretches of the number line: besides arithmetic and digit rules (and rule-plus-exception concepts), the only numerical concept they consider is "numbers within some distance of one of the examples I saw", with smaller similarity radii a priori likelier, weighed by the same tempered, exception-tolerant size principle. So endorsement of a non-rule target falls off with its numerical distance to the nearest example, whatever lies between the examples: an empty gap between two distant examples is not filled in, while each example's own close neighbours are endorsed even when they lie outside the span of the set.

name: conservative_belief_reporting
hypothesis: People infer the program's concept just as the best Bayesian concept learner does, but they report their belief conservatively: when deciding whether to answer "yes", they hedge toward fifty-fifty, so their odds of saying yes are a compressed (less extreme) version of their belief's odds, by a fitted degree of conservatism. Targets they are fairly but not fully sure belong (or do not belong) are therefore endorsed (or rejected) less consistently than their belief implies, with no lapses and no overall lean toward yes or no.

name: salient_contained_digit_rules
hypothesis: Refinement of `gamma_shaped_range_width_prior`: people do the same tempered, exception-tolerant Bayesian concept learning (salient final-digit rules, ranges on a compressed number line with a gamma-shaped width prior, and rule-plus-neighbourhood exceptions anchored on an off-pattern example and emitted through a side channel), but rules about a digit the numeral contains ("has a 4 in it") are also perceptually salient. They are read straight off the written numerals, so they get their own fitted prior boost instead of starting no more likely than an arbitrary arithmetic rule. The one change is this contained-digit salience: when every example contains a common digit in different places, people extend that digit to distant numbers that contain it (especially numbers in that digit's decade, such as 47 after 34, 43, 74), more than the incumbent predicts (the critique's shared-contained-digit tens statistic).

hypothesis: Refinement of `range_plus_exception_side_channel`: people do the same tempered, exception-tolerant Bayesian concept learning (salient final-digit rules, ranges on a compressed number line, rule-plus-neighbourhood exceptions anchored on an off-pattern example and emitted through a side channel) and also entertain "range plus exception" programs ("numbers from 20 to 35, and now and then something around 87"), but their prior expectation of how wide a range is — for plain ranges and for the main range of a range-plus-exception program alike — is not the fixed Erlang shape that makes ranges of one or two numbers unlikely, but a gamma shape whose shape is fitted (grafted from `gamma_shaped_range_width_prior`). The one change is this free-shaped width prior: if people find tight ranges plausible, they generalise steeply to the close neighbours of a lone example or tight cluster, and when most examples cluster and one lies far away they fill in only a narrow stretch around the cluster, endorse the outlier's close neighbours, and reject the gap between them.

name: pedagogical_teacher_gamma_width
hypothesis: Refinement of `pedagogical_teacher_sampling`: people assume the examples were picked by a helpful teacher who chose numbers that point unambiguously to the program (so an ambiguous "special" number such as 16 or 64 is strong evidence for the rule it is special for and weak evidence for a mere range around it), and otherwise do the same tempered, exception-tolerant concept learning over salient final-digit and other rules, ranges, and rule-plus-neighbourhood exceptions anchored on an off-pattern example and emitted through a side channel. The one change, grafted from `gamma_shaped_range_width_prior`, is their prior expectation of how wide a "range of numbers" program is: not the fixed Erlang shape that makes ranges of one or two numbers unlikely, but a gamma shape whose shape is fitted, so that when a helpful teacher shows unremarkable numbers people may read them as pointing to a tight range hugging the examples and generalise steeply to close neighbours, while special numbers still pull them towards the rules they exemplify.

name: salient_repdigit_concept
hypothesis: People do the same tempered, exception-tolerant Bayesian concept learning as the best model (salient final-digit and contained-digit rules, ranges on a compressed number line, and rule-plus-neighbourhood exceptions around an off-pattern example), but their space of concepts also includes "numbers written with a repeated digit" (11, 22, 33, … 99). They read this visually striking pattern straight off the numerals and find it far more plausible a priori than an arbitrary arithmetic rule. So when the examples include doubled-digit numbers, people extend to other repdigits far away (such as 44 or 77) and endorse near neighbours that break the doubling less than the best model predicts.

name: independent_feature_prototype
hypothesis: People do not search a space of rules or ranges; they summarise the examples as a single category prototype — a central tendency with a spread on a compressed mental number line, plus how often each final digit and each parity occurred among the examples (shrunk toward an even spread by prior uncertainty) — and say "yes" in proportion to how typical the target is of that prototype relative to a number picked at random. Each feature is judged independently, so a target is endorsed if it lies within the examples' magnitude spread and shares their dominant parity and final digit, and the prototype tightens smoothly as more consistent examples accumulate.

name: generative_production_odds_judgement
hypothesis: People answer not by asking whether the target belongs to the concept they inferred, but by imagining the program running and judging how likely it is to produce that very number compared with a number picked at random; the larger this production-to-chance ratio, the more likely they say yes (their concept inference is the same tempered, exception-tolerant Bayesian learning as the best model). So a target from a small concept (a tight range around the examples, a sparse rule, the neighbourhood of an off-pattern example) is endorsed more than an equally certain member of a broad concept such as "even numbers", and people extend broad rules to distant numbers less than their membership belief alone implies.

name: salient_decade_place_value_rules
hypothesis: Refinement of `salient_contained_digit_rules`: people do the same tempered, exception-tolerant Bayesian concept learning (salient final-digit and contained-digit rules, ranges on a compressed number line with a gamma-shaped width prior, and rule-plus-neighbourhood exceptions anchored on an off-pattern example and emitted through a side channel), but they also read the tens digit of a numeral as a place-value category: "numbers in the forties" (tens digit 4) is a rule they entertain directly, with its own fitted salience, not only as one range among the thousands of possible stretches of the number line. The one change is this set of salient decade rules: when the examples share a tens digit (e.g. 42, 47, 45), people fill in exactly that decade, endorsing its members, even those far from any example, and rejecting numbers just across the decade boundary (39, 50) more sharply than a learner whose only magnitude concepts are ranges with arbitrary edges.

name: individual_rule_vs_range_style
hypothesis: Refinement of `salient_contained_digit_rules`: people do the same tempered, exception-tolerant Bayesian concept learning (salient final-digit and contained-digit rules, ranges on a compressed number line with a gamma-shaped width prior, and rule-plus-neighbourhood exceptions emitted through a side channel), but individuals differ stably in how readily they think of the hidden program as an arithmetic or digit rule rather than a range of magnitudes. The one change is this person-specific prior share for rules versus ranges, fitted for each person: some participants consistently extend shared rules to distant numbers, while others consistently stay near the examples' stretch of the number line across every set they judge.
